questions.question: Who first introduced ridge regression, and in which year?
questions.gold: Hoerl and Kennard introduced the theory in 1970.

answers.A: Ridge regression was first introduced by Arthur E. Hoerl and Robert W. Kennard in 1970. They published their seminal paper, "Ridge Regression: Biased Estimation for Nonorthogonal Problems," in the journal *Technometrics*. This method was developed to address the issue of multicollinearity in multiple linear regression models.
answers.B: Ridge regression was first introduced by Hoerl and Kennard in 1970 [p002]. They presented the theory in their Technometrics papers titled "Ridge regressions: biased estimation of nonorthogonal problems" and "Ridge regressions: applications in nonorthogonal problems" [p002].
answers.C: Ridge regression was first introduced by Hoerl and Kennard in 1970 [p002]. They presented the theory in their Technometrics papers titled "Ridge regressions: biased estimation of nonorthogonal problems" and "Ridge regressions: applications in nonorthogonal problems" [p002].

questions.question: How does k-fold cross-validation split the data?
questions.gold: The sample is randomly partitioned into k equal-sized folds; one fold is kept as validation data and the other k-1 folds are used for training.

answers.A: K-fold cross-validation randomly partitions the original dataset into $k$ equal-sized subsets, or "folds." The model is then trained $k$ times, each time using $k-1$ folds for training and the remaining single fold for validation. This process ensures that every data point is used for both training and testing exactly once. Finally, the performance metrics from each iteration are averaged to produce a single estimation of the model's predictive power.
answers.B: In k-fold cross-validation, the original sample is randomly partitioned into k equal sized subsamples, often referred to as "folds" [p051]. Of these k subsamples, a single subsample is retained as the validation data for testing the model [p051]. The remaining k − 1 subsamples are used as training data [p051].
answers.C: In k-fold cross-validation, the original sample is randomly partitioned into k equal sized subsamples, often referred to as "folds" [p051]. Of these k subsamples, a single subsample is retained as the validation data for testing the model [p051]. The remaining k − 1 subsamples are used as training data [p051].

questions.question: What goes wrong in gradient descent if the step size is too large?

answers.A: If the step size is too large, gradient descent may overshoot the minimum of the loss function. This can cause the algorithm to oscillate around the optimum or diverge entirely, leading to increasing error values instead of convergence. Consequently, the model fails to find the optimal parameters and the training process becomes unstable.
answers.B: If the step size is too large, it leads to overshoot and divergence [p093].
answers.C: If the step size is too large, it leads to overshoot and divergence [p093].

questions.question: Why can the parameters not be estimated under perfect multicollinearity?
questions.gold: The design matrix has less than full rank, so the moment matrix cannot be inverted and the system has infinitely many solutions.

answers.A: Under perfect multicollinearity, the independent variables are linearly dependent, causing the design matrix to be singular and its determinant to be zero. Consequently, the inverse of the matrix $X'X$ does not exist, which is required to compute the Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) estimator. Without this inverse, there is no unique solution for the regression coefficients, making them impossible to estimate.
answers.B: Under perfect multicollinearity, the design matrix has less than full rank because the predictive variables have an exact linear relationship [p069]. Consequently, the moment matrix cannot be inverted [p069]. This mathematical limitation means the system of equations has infinitely many solutions [p069]. Therefore, the parameter estimates of the regression are not well-defined [p069].
answers.C: Under perfect multicollinearity, the design matrix has less than full rank because the predictive variables have an exact linear relationship [p069]. Consequently, the moment matrix cannot be inverted [p069]. This mathematical limitation means the system of equations has infinitely many solutions [p069]. Therefore, the parameter estimates of the regression are not well-defined [p069].

questions.question: Which statistician popularised the method that, in the 'large p, small n' case, selects at most n variables before it saturates, and in which year?
questions.gold: Robert Tibshirani popularised the lasso in 1996.

answers.A: The statistician is Robert Tibshirani, who popularized the Lasso (Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator) method. He introduced this technique in his seminal 1996 paper titled "Regression Shrinkage and Selection via the Lasso." The Lasso is well-known for its property of selecting at most $n$ variables when the number of predictors $p$ exceeds the number of observations $n$, due to the geometric constraints of the $\ell_1$ penalty.
answers.B: The method that selects at most n variables before saturating in the "large p, small n" case is LASSO [p015]. Statistician Robert Tibshirani independently rediscovered and popularized this method [p006]. He did so in 1996 [p006].
answers.C: The method described is Lasso, which selects at most n variables before saturating in the "large p, small n" case [p015]. Statistician Robert Tibshirani independently rediscovered and popularized this method [p006]. He did so in 1996 [p006].

questions.question: Which techniques does the overfitting article list for lessening overfitting, and which of them does the decision tree article call necessary for trees?
questions.gold: The overfitting article lists model comparison, cross-validation, regularization, early stopping, pruning, Bayesian priors and dropout; the decision tree article says pruning is necessary for trees.

answers.A: Common techniques for reducing overfitting include regularization, early stopping, cross-validation, and pruning. While general methods like regularization apply to many models, the decision tree algorithm specifically relies on pruning to prevent excessive complexity. Therefore, pruning is the technique identified as necessary for decision trees to mitigate overfitting effectively.
answers.B: The provided sources do not contain an "overfitting article" or a distinct "decision tree article," but rather excerpts from a single text. Source [p127] states that mechanisms such as pruning are necessary to avoid overfitting in decision-tree learners, with the exception of algorithms like the Conditional Inference approach. It also mentions that methods such as the dual information distance (DID) tree were proposed to reduce the greedy effect of local optimality. Therefore, based on the available text, pruning is identified as the necessary mechanism for avoiding overfitting in standard decision trees [p127].
answers.C: The article on overfitting lists model comparison, cross-validation, regularization, early stopping, pruning, Bayesian priors, and dropout as techniques to lessen overfitting [p031]. The decision tree article states that mechanisms such as pruning are necessary to avoid the problem of overfitting in decision-tree learners [p127]. However, it notes an exception for algorithms like the Conditional Inference approach, which does not require pruning [p127][p122].

questions.question: How do the lasso and the elastic net behave differently on a group of highly correlated variables?
questions.gold: The lasso tends to select one variable from the group and ignore the others; the elastic net has a grouping effect that gives correlated features equal weights.

answers.A: When faced with a group of highly correlated variables, the lasso tends to arbitrarily select just one variable from the group while shrinking the coefficients of the others to zero. In contrast, the elastic net encourages a grouping effect, where strongly correlated predictors are either included in or excluded from the model together. This behavior arises because the elastic net combines the $L_1$ penalty of the lasso with the $L_2$ penalty of ridge regression, which stabilizes the selection process. Consequently, the elastic net is generally preferred over the lasso when multicollinearity is present, as it provides more stable and interpretable models.
answers.B: When dealing with a group of highly correlated variables, the LASSO tends to select only one variable from the group while ignoring the others [p015]. In contrast, the elastic net overcomes this limitation by adding a quadratic penalty term to the LASSO's penalty function [p016]. This modification allows the elastic net to handle groups of correlated variables more effectively than the standard LASSO approach [p015][p016].
answers.C: When dealing with a group of highly correlated variables, the LASSO tends to select only one variable from the group and ignore the others [p015]. In contrast, the elastic net overcomes this limitation by adding a quadratic penalty term to the LASSO's penalty function [p016]. This modification allows the elastic net to include multiple correlated variables rather than just selecting a single representative [p015][p016]. Consequently, the elastic net provides a more stable solution in high-dimensional settings where LASSO might saturate or arbitrarily pick variables [p015][p016].

questions.question: How does the holdout method differ from k-fold cross-validation?
questions.gold: The holdout method assigns data to one training and one test set and runs once; k-fold cross-validation rotates through k folds and averages multiple runs.

answers.A: The holdout method splits the dataset into a single training set and a single test set, whereas k-fold cross-validation partitions the data into k subsets and iteratively trains on k-1 folds while testing on the remaining one. This means holdout uses only one specific split for evaluation, which can lead to high variance depending on how the data is divided. In contrast, k-fold cross-validation averages performance across all k iterations, providing a more robust and reliable estimate of model generalization. Consequently, cross-validation makes better use of limited data compared to the simpler holdout approach.
answers.B: In the holdout method, data is randomly assigned to two sets, a training set and a test set, involving only a single run of model testing [p052]. In contrast, k-fold cross-validation partitions the original sample into k equal sized subsamples, or folds [p051]. For each iteration in k-fold cross-validation, one subsample is retained as validation data while the remaining k − 1 subsamples are used for training [p051]. Unlike the single run of the holdout method, typical cross-validation averages the results of multiple runs of model-testing together [p052].
answers.C: The holdout method involves a single run where data is randomly split into a training set and a test set [p052]. In contrast, k-fold cross-validation partitions the original sample into k equal-sized subsamples, or folds [p051]. For each iteration of k-fold cross-validation, one subsample is used for validation while the remaining k-1 subsamples serve as training data [p051]. Unlike the holdout method, typical cross-validation averages the results of multiple runs of model testing [p052].
